text: Jesus called the Twelve together and gave them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases.
Then he sent them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal the sick.
He told them, "Take nothing for the journey — no staff, no bag, no bread, no money, and no extra shirt.
Whatever house you enter, stay there, and leave from there.
And wherever people do not welcome you, leave that town and shake the dust from your feet as a testimony against them."
So they set out and went from village to village, proclaiming the good news and healing everywhere.
Herod the tetrarch heard about everything that was happening, and he was perplexed, because some were saying that John had been raised from the dead,
others that Elijah had appeared, and still others that one of the prophets of long ago had risen.
But Herod said, "I beheaded John. So who is this man I hear such things about?" And he kept trying to see him.
When the apostles returned, they told him everything they had done. Then he took them with him and withdrew privately to a town called Bethsaida.
But the crowds found out and followed him. He welcomed them, spoke to them about the kingdom of God, and healed those who needed healing.
Late in the day the Twelve came to him and said, "Send the crowd away, so they can go to the surrounding villages and countryside to find lodging and food, because we are here in a deserted place."
But he said to them, "You give them something to eat." They answered, "We have no more than five loaves and two fish — unless we go and buy food for all these people."
There were about five thousand men. He said to his disciples, "Have them sit down in groups of about fifty."
They did so, and had them all sit down.

versions.text: They did so, and everyone sat down.
versions.explanation: The Greek verb κατέκλιναν is active with the disciples as subject and ἅπαντας ('all of them') as object: the disciples made everyone recline. The current rendering turns it into an intransitive action by the crowd, losing the disciples' obedience to the command in v. 14.

text: Then he took the five loaves and the two fish, looked up to heaven, blessed them, broke them, and kept giving them to the disciples to set before the crowd.
They all ate and were satisfied, and the pieces left over were picked up — twelve baskets full.
Once, while he was praying alone and his disciples were with him, he asked them, "Who do the crowds say I am?"
They answered, "John the Baptist; others say Elijah; and still others that one of the prophets of long ago has risen."
"But what about you?" he asked. "Who do you say I am?" Peter answered, "The Christ of God."
Jesus warned them sternly not to tell this to anyone.
"The Son of Man must suffer many things," he said, "and be rejected by the elders, the chief priests, and the scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised."
Then he said to them all: "If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me.
For whoever wants to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will save it.
What good is it for someone to gain the whole world and yet lose or forfeit his very self?
Whoever is ashamed of me and my words, the Son of Man will be ashamed of him when he comes in his glory and in the glory of the Father and of the holy angels.
Truly I tell you, there are some standing here who will not taste death before they see the kingdom of God."
About eight days after saying this, Jesus took Peter, John, and James with him and went up on the mountain to pray.
As he was praying, the appearance of his face changed, and his clothing became dazzling white.
And suddenly two men were talking with him — Moses and Elijah.
They appeared in glory and spoke about his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.
Peter and his companions were heavy with sleep, but when they came fully awake, they saw his glory and the two men standing with him.

As the men were leaving him, Peter said to Jesus, "Master, it is good for us to be here. Let us put up three shelters — one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah." He did not know what he was saying.
While he was speaking, a cloud came and overshadowed them, and they were afraid as they entered the cloud.
And a voice came from the cloud, saying, "This is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him!"
When the voice had spoken, they found Jesus alone. And they kept silent, telling no one in those days anything of what they had seen.

versions.text: When the voice had spoken, they found Jesus alone. And they kept silent, telling no one at that time anything of what they had seen.
versions.explanation: ἐν ἐκείναις ταῖς ἡμέραις is a plural time expression, 'in those days', indicating an extended period of silence rather than a single moment; 'at that time' narrows the sense.

text: The next day, when they came down from the mountain, a large crowd met him.
A man in the crowd cried out, "Teacher, I beg you, look at my son — he is my only child.
A spirit seizes him, and suddenly he screams; it throws him into convulsions so that he foams at the mouth. It leaves him only with great difficulty, and it mauls him as it goes.

versions.text: A spirit seizes him, and suddenly he screams; it throws him into convulsions so that he foams at the mouth. It hardly ever leaves him, and it is destroying him.
versions.explanation: μόγις ἀποχωρεῖ means it departs 'only with difficulty' on each occasion, not that it seldom leaves; and συντρῖβον αὐτόν is a participle describing the violence with which it goes out ('mauling/shattering him'). The revised wording keeps the oral rhythm while matching the Greek.

text: I begged your disciples to drive it out, but they could not."
Jesus answered, "You unbelieving and perverse generation, how long must I be with you and put up with you? Bring your son here."
Even as the boy was coming, the demon threw him to the ground in convulsions. But Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit, healed the boy, and gave him back to his father.
They were all astonished at the majesty of God. While everyone was marveling at all that he was doing, he said to his disciples,
"Let these words sink deep into your ears: the Son of Man is about to be delivered into human hands."

versions.text: "Listen carefully and take these words to heart: the Son of Man is going to be delivered into human hands."
versions.explanation: The Greek idiom is literally 'put these words into your ears,' a vivid command that the current rendering flattens into a generic paraphrase ('take to heart' suggests the heart, not the ears). Retaining the ear-imagery keeps the force of the original and still reads well aloud. 'Is about to' also better captures μέλλει.

text: But they did not understand this saying; it was hidden from them so that they could not grasp it, and they were afraid to ask him about it.
An argument arose among them about which of them was the greatest.
Knowing the thoughts of their hearts, Jesus took a little child and had him stand at his side.

versions.text: Knowing the thoughts of their hearts, Jesus took a little child and stood him beside himself.
versions.explanation: 'Stood him beside himself' is awkward for oral reading and the reflexive can be momentarily misheard. 'Had him stand at his side' is smoother and equally accurate.

text: Then he said to them, "Whoever welcomes this little child in my name welcomes me, and whoever welcomes me welcomes the one who sent me. For the one who is least among you all — he is the one who is great."
John answered, "Master, we saw someone driving out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he does not follow along with us."

versions.text: John said, "Master, we saw someone driving out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he is not one of us who follow you."
versions.explanation: The participle Ἀποκριθεὶς ('answering/responding') is dropped; it marks John's remark as a response to what Jesus just said. Also 'not one of us who follow you' shifts the object of following to Jesus, whereas the Greek says he does not follow 'with us' — the disciples' concern is that he is outside their circle.

text: "Do not stop him," Jesus said to him, "for whoever is not against you is for you."
As the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face resolutely to go to Jerusalem,
and he sent messengers on ahead. They went into a Samaritan village to make preparations for him,
but the people there would not receive him, because he was heading for Jerusalem.
When the disciples James and John saw this, they said, "Lord, do you want us to call down fire from heaven to destroy them?"
But he turned and rebuked them.
And they went on to another village.
As they were walking along the road, someone said to him, "I will follow you wherever you go."
Jesus replied, "Foxes have dens and birds of the sky have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head."
He said to another, "Follow me." But the man replied, "Lord, let me go and bury my father first."
Jesus said to him, "Let the dead bury their own dead. You go and proclaim the kingdom of God."
Still another said, "I will follow you, Lord, but first let me say farewell to those at my home."
Jesus said, "No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God."

versions.text: Jesus said to him, "No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God."
versions.explanation: The text reads simply 'Jesus said'; 'to him' is added content not supported by the reading followed here.
